newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Focus - Sweden to say yes to EMU, but in 2003 - poll.
newsitem.headline: Focus - Sweden to say yes to EMU, but in 2003 - poll.

text.p: Sweden's ruling Social Democrat party will probably agree to join European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), but in 2003 and not in the first wave in 1999, analysts polled by Reuters said on Thursday.
The survey of 10 analysts in Stockholm and London showed they believed the chances of Sweden saying yes to membership in 2003 was, on average, 51 percent.
The probability of Sweden saying yes to joining in 2001 was 32.5 percent, which was the second most likely scenario expected by analysts, the poll showed.
The chance of a yes after 2003 was 11.5 percent and for a yes from EMU's start in 1999 was 3.5 percent. A flat out no to EMU was only seen having a remote 1.5 percent probability.

Leaders of Sweden's Social Democrat party are expected to reveal their view soon, possibly as early as Friday when the party's executive committee meets, although officials were circumspect on Thursday on when its ruling party would reveal its position.
Prime Minister Goran Persson's office referred questions about when the country would give its opinion on EMU to the finance ministry.
But a spokeswoman for Finance Minister Erik Asbrink said she did not know any details about an announcement.
"I assume there will be a press conference, or some kind of meeting or seminar," the spokeswoman told Reuters.
Asbrink's spokeswoman has said the minister would advise markets at least a few hours before he announces his decision.
Persson said on Wednesday an announcement would be made on Friday or next week, but added that this was not definite and the statement could be even later.

Some analysts said their forecasts on the likelihood of Sweden joining EMU were influenced by a radio report earlier this week which said Persson and Asbrink had agreed Sweden could not join EMU during the current parliamentary term.

Analysts said this report, broadcast on Wednesday, meant Swedish EMU membership would be delayed until after the next general election in 2002 unless the government held an extra election during the 1998-2002 mandate period.
However, holding a special election like this not normal practice in Sweden and political analysts said it was unlikely to take place.
Leaks like this are common in Sweden, and the debt market took this leak as a signal to weaken slightly, but it recovered slightly when the finance ministry dismissed the report as speculation.
"Because of the possible leak which we had yesterday, the chances have increased of the answer being more negative than was earlier expected," said Swedbank analyst Peter Granqvist.
"We are now expecting a 'soft yes' -- meaning membership in 2001 or a 'soft no' -- meaning membership in 2003."
Aragon brokerage economist Anders Hahnel also believed a Swedish membership in EMU would be postponed.
"We believe the government will formulate its view with a wait-and-see statement. The Social Democrats do not want to say yes or no without having the entire party behind it."
"They also may not necessarily pinpoint a year, but instead say they will join when the crown is stabilised and when they bring down a high state debt and high unemployment," he added.

Analysts say Sweden risks losing influence within the European Union and being grouped with countries such as Portugal, Italy and Greece if it elects to stay outside the first wave of countries to sign up.
"International developments put Sweden at risk of being in a difficult situation if we wait so long," Handelsbanken Chief Economist Carl B Hamilton told Reuters.
"Many countries will join in the second wave and there will be a lot of pressure for Sweden to join as well."

He said if British Prime Minister Tony Blair makes the preparations to join, Sweden must not move at a slower pace, "or we will risk being outside together with countries like Greece, which is something I don't think any Swedish politician wants".
